I live in Milan and work in fashion. I followed the shoot through local press and saw a lot of it in person — sometimes in plain sight, sometimes low-key, sometimes completely under the radar.

That specific Miranda scene at the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II still gives me chills. I was there, outside, at 3 a.m.

They shot it during last summer’s Fashion Week on purpose — that’s when Milan is full of the right energy and the right faces. Around 2,000 extras were pulled straight from the city.

text:
I’m a big fan of the first film, so I was really excited when I heard there might be a second one. Ever since the first trailer dropped, I’ve been looking forward to it. I even planned to get my partner—who almost never watches films—to finally see the original this weekend so we could go to see the new one together next Friday. And yet, it took one 30-second clip to completely ruin that excitement.

What I saw wasn’t just disappointing—it was offensive. The way this Asian character is portrayed is not okay. The name sounds far too close to the racial slur that I, and many others, have actually been called in real life. On top of that, the whole “nerdy Asian” stereotype feels lazy and outdated.

It’s completely out of touch with reality. In my own workplace, when my new Chinese assistants join, the comments they get are about how stylish they are—things like “where do they get their cute outfits?” or “their makeup is amazing.” That’s the real impression people have, not this tired stereotype being pushed on screen.

And that’s exactly why this feels so unacceptable. This isn’t some small, low-budget project getting it wrong—it’s a major film backed by names like Meryl Streep, Anne Hathaway, Emily Blunt, and Stanley Tucci. There is simply no excuse. In 2026, with all the conversations around representation and respect, putting something like this on screen shows a complete lack of awareness and care. text: Overrated, in my opinion. Felt stale and like it belonged to a bygone era - or, maybe, like it was a passion project started years ago and quickly finished recently. I vividly remember only one song from the entire score (the one where Andy's boyfriend sings that he loves her body) - and I thought: wow, you can really hear the good old Elton in it! I wish I could remember any other songs, but they were all forgettable... Vanessa Williams looked very elegant and swooshed her coats like a perfect Miranda would, but I'm not sure if overall she sang all that much - I definitely don't remember any out-of-tune notes, but maybe it's because there were no actual songs, not sure. Most of the act two the audience around me kept yawning - it really felt like watching a weirdly converted, sped up movie without any time to really let the action sink in. I remember most of the costumes were very pretty - especially the ones in the met gala scene - but overall, I am really not surprised that the show is constantly available on discounted ticket pages.

text:
Saw this past week on a trip to London (visiting from California.) Perhaps an unpopular opinion, but I didn’t like it. Other than Vanessa Williams, who was perfect in the role and did it justice (she’s better than the show), I feel it’s in need of some rewriting and recasting. Over sung - shrill in some cases, over acted - especially by the Emily and Andrea leads, and the stage adaptation of the book fell flat for me. Some positives though, the ensemble were fabulous and well choreographed (they too had amazing voices), the sets were clever, and while the Emily and Andrea characters over sung their parts - they had amazing voices and control over their instrument. Perhaps it was just the night I saw it, but the onstage chemistry wasn’t there. My partner and I commented as we were leaving the theatre, this show will not make it in New York. Not that it has to, but I would think the producers would love to see success in London and then take it to other major markets, like New York. I just don’t see wide commercial success for this musical version of the production. Here’s hoping they prove me wrong. I expect more from Elton John; I think he was lazy with this one and made it sound too much like Mama Mia. Was I the only one who thought the cast was going to burst into a rendition of Masquerade on the gala staircase? 😂

Thank you for posting your thoughtful review here on YT, MickeyJo. I appreciate your thorough analysis. We may not agree on some of the points for this production, I respect your take and well stated opinions.

text:
When I heard they were going to make a musical, my first thought was DO-NOT-TOUCH-THAT-MOVIE!!! But… I was there last week at the opening night in the Dominion Theatre and I must say I was very pleasantly surprised. I fully agree the cast is excellent, staging and set design top, outfits top. 

Regarding music: some numbers (e.g. I only love you for your body) are 100% Elton-style, others may be more difficult to be recognized as his compositions. The refrain of the number „Runway“ sung by Emily reminds me of „Somewhere“ from West Side Story - I really hope it‘s not going to turn out to be a plagiarism… 

Regarding singing: generally very good, except the high note at the end of The Devil wears Prada (the ball scene) sung by someone from the cast and which was totally off-pitch/flat and really hurt my ears. They should work a bit more on that one with their vocal coach. 

I was also glad that they kept a lot of the original text from the movie. Especially Miranda’s famous cerulean-monologue was kept almost in its entirety. However, I was missing the equally famous „Florals? For spring?! Groundbreaking!“ 

Also, they added some additional story lines like Emily‘s flirting with the nurses in the hospital where she is hospitalized following her accident (Bon Voyage). This is something which is not in the original movie but nevertheless a good idea as an 11 o‘clock number.


Overall, a very positive experience.

They absolutely didn’t cut Andy’s friends due to “budget restraints on cast members…” this is already a huge cast. The friends would be doubled with some of the ensemble-members; this is JUST a (sadly expected) case of bad-writing, and excluding essential character building, in favor of more time toward generic “pop” music.
OH/// and the Vanessa Williams/ Miranda situation is extremely common —- I assume that Williams contract (or at least her agreement) hinged on the fact that her character would have a particular amount of stage time and songs.
AND as far as her bow, this is expected. NO ONE would have thought that she was not going to get the last bow —- the last bow generally is going to be given to the person who will get the biggest audience-response, otherwise you will have screams and people leaping to their feet… then when the next person comes on, the entire reception falls — THIS feels bad for the show and the cast.
SO, in your high school production the lead character will probably always bow last. On Broadway, it will almost always be the biggest “Star”.

text: What's interesting about this show is that in the movie, Miranda is like this perfect puzzle piece that makes the movie as great as it is. However when it comes to the musical, she's the one drawback. Everyone else is actually pretty fitting for the stage, they're campy and ridiculous enough to break into song and dance. I think Vanessa Williams is doing well in what is a really tough job as an actor. Not only is she playing a character that isn't built for the stage, but she also can't deviate too much from Meryl's original performance, lest the character become unrecognisable. text: The Nightworkers--- an ode to the duality of the office and its forgotten workers: the blue collar workers often not seen in the course of the typical work day but only at night-- the mail room crew, the security guards, the cleaning/janitorial staff, building maintenance, and the white collar office workers who, in the process of working late on this or that project, shed their formal workday selves as they work into the night. This collection and the runway song  they chose evokes that weird dream space of late night working and workers.  The song is called "Moments in Love" by Art of Noise and in the 1980s and 90s, this song began most "Quiet Storm" radio shows around the U.S. and some abroad as well. "Quiet Storm" radio shows were often featured on R&B stations as an accompaniment to the night. The shows presented quiet reflective music, often romantic ballads and jazz. Yes, you would listen to Quiet Storm shows with a lover, but they were also just the soundtrack to late night working and studying. It's a very nuanced and, as usual for Prada, a very intellectual collection. I enjoyed it.

text: It seems like the collection is a juxtaposition of different leisure ideologies. Like the flower rugs contrasted against its nature, on concrete with light coming through square windows. Prada is very much about tailoring, and its politics, see Miucia Prada. If you look at the green military knit, it appears to be the expected military codes of Prada, but it’s finished with a tasseled hem. It’s a harsh line to contrast against military shoulders. And in the design lines contrast is where I find the cultural interpretation. The military shoulders feel calm but the tassels are what startles and reverses the roles of soft and hard in clothing culture.
